places.name: Alexandria

visits.text: The Bibliotheca Alexandrina building alone is worth the trip. Its glass roof, tilted toward the sea like a sundial, covers a reading room with eleven cascading levels. The gray granite walls bear characters from 120 writing systems. Opened in 2002, the library also houses four museums and a planetarium. Tickets for the Antiquities Museum, which displays about 1,300 objects, are sold separately. Tours and museums: Sunday through Thursday, 9:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.; Saturday, 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.

The Citadel of Qaitbay occupies the site of the Lighthouse of Alexandria, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. This lighthouse, reputed to have stood 138 m tall, was completely destroyed by two earthquakes, in 1303 and 1323. Sultan Qaitbay, who ruled Egypt at the time, had the fortress built between 1477 and 1479 at the entrance to the Eastern Harbor. After 1952, the Egyptian navy established a maritime museum here. Arrive early in the morning to explore the seaward ramparts before the tour groups.

A large dome, four smaller ones, and a minaret about 73 m tall rise above the Abu al-Abbas al-Mursi Mosque in the Anfoushi district. It honors a Sufi mystic, a master of Islamic spirituality, who died in 1286. King Fuad I commissioned the current building in 1934, and it was completed around 1945. Its style imitates that of the Mamluks, the sultans who ruled Egypt in the late Middle Ages. Admire it from the esplanade and avoid the main Friday noon prayer.

Though small, the Roman theater at Kom el-Dikka is the heart of Alexandria’s most complete ancient site visible in the open air. Its tiered seating dates from the 4th century and is made of marble salvaged from other monuments. Around it, some twenty lecture halls formed a kind of university from the 5th to the 7th century: each held 20 to 30 students. Leave time for the Villa of the Birds: its mosaic of nine birds in nine squares remains where it was originally laid.

An Italian-style palace built in 1926, formerly the United States consulate, has housed the Alexandria National Museum since 2003. Its roughly 1,800 objects are arranged chronologically, with one level for each major period. The first presents pharaonic Egypt, with mummies in a reconstructed burial chamber. The second covers the Greek and Roman periods, including objects from Heracleion and Canopus, two ancient cities in the region. The third spans Coptic and Islamic art through the 20th century: visit them in order.

Alexandria’s Greco-Roman Museum alone deserves a morning. First opened in 1892, it reopened in October 2023 after nearly eighteen years of renovation. More than 25 galleries display statues of Alexander the Great and the Ptolemies, the Greek kings who ruled Egypt after him. Also look for the Tanagra statuettes, small terracotta figurines, and objects recovered from the seabed. Allow 2 hours, before the afternoon heat.

A spiral staircase descends into the rock to the Catacombs of Kom el-Shuqafa, carved out in the 2nd century to house the dead. They were rediscovered in 1900 when a donkey fell into the access shaft. On the walls, Anubis, the jackal-headed god who guided the dead, wears the armor of a Roman soldier: Egypt was then a province of Rome, and beliefs were blending. Near the entrance, the triclinium is a banquet hall where families ate during funerals. Wear shoes with good traction.

Pompey’s Pillar never honored the Roman general Pompey. It was erected around AD 300 in honor of Emperor Diocletian. Its name stems from a misreading: European travelers confused the name of the man who dedicated it in the Greek inscription with Pompey’s. Standing nearly 27 m tall, it towers over the ruins of the Serapeum, the ancient temple of the god Serapis. Its shaft, carved from a single block of pink granite, comes from Aswan. Continue to the nearby catacombs.

You’ll end the day at the Royal Jewelry Museum in the Zizinia neighborhood. It occupies the palace of Princess Fatma al-Zahra, built in 1919. Its display cases hold jewelry belonging to the Muhammad Ali dynasty, the family that ruled Egypt from 1805 to 1952. The palace itself also deserves attention, with its 19th-century paintings, statues, and art objects. Allow 1 hour 15 minutes.

On your way back from Rosetta, you’ll stop at Montaza Gardens, the former royal estate east of Alexandria. The park covers about 120 hectares. King Fuad I had Haramlek Palace built here in 1932, combining Ottoman and Florentine styles. Walk to the waterfront, overlooked by the palace. There is an admission fee for the park.

activities.text: If you arrive before sunset, walk along Alexandria’s Corniche, the waterfront promenade bordering the Eastern Harbor. It stretches for about 17 km, from the Bahary district in the west to Mandara in the east. From the Bibliotheca, head west: at the far end of the bay, you will see the Citadel of Qaitbay, which you will visit the next day.

For your final evening, nothing beats a fish dinner in Alexandria, a city renowned for its seafood restaurants. At popular restaurants, fish is often priced by weight. Ask for the price per kilo before it is cooked to avoid surprises. The next day, Borg El Arab Airport is 45 km to the southwest, and direct trains reach Cairo in about 2 hours 40 minutes to 3 hours.

visits.text: Drive from Luxor to Aswan (220 km) with two major stops. First stop: the temple of Edfu, dedicated to the falcon god Horus, is the best-preserved Ptolemaic temple in Egypt—and the second largest after Karnak. Built between 237 and 57 BC, it took 180 years to complete. Its entrance pylon, 36 meters high, bears reliefs showing Ptolemy XII smiting his enemies before Horus. Inside, the hypostyle hall with 18 columns is intact, with its ceiling still in place—which is extremely rare. Plan 1 to 1.5 hours for the visit.

Second stop: the Temple of Kom Ombo, about 40 km from Aswan, a 40-minute drive, stands spectacularly on a promontory overlooking the Nile. Its unique feature is that it is a double temple, dedicated simultaneously to two deities - Sobek (the crocodile god) on the south side and Haroeris (Horus the Elder) on the north side. Everything is symmetrical: two entrances, two sanctuaries, two series of reliefs. On the outer wall, do not miss the panel showing surgical instruments - one of the rare depictions of ancient medicine. The small adjoining Crocodile Museum displays mummified Nile crocodiles found in the surrounding area. Allow 45 minutes to 1 hour.

The temple of Philae, dedicated to the goddess Isis, is one of Egypt's most beautiful Ptolemaic temples—and its setting is unique. Built between 380 BC and the 3rd century AD, it stands on an island accessible only by water taxi (10-15 minutes from the Shellal dock). The temple's recent history is as extraordinary as the ancient: threatened with submersion by rising waters after construction of the Aswan High Dam, it was entirely dismantled stone by stone then reassembled on neighboring Agilkia Island between 1972 and 1980 as part of a UNESCO international campaign. Trajan's Kiosk, with its 14 columns all with different capitals, is Aswan's most photographed structure. Plan 2 to 2.5 hours including the boat crossing.

The Unfinished Obelisk, in the pink granite quarries of Aswan south of the city, is a giant obelisk abandoned during carving—probably commissioned by Hatshepsut around 1450 BC. Had it been completed, it would have measured 42 meters and weighed 1,200 tons, making it Egypt's largest obelisk. A crack discovered in the rock forced the carvers to abandon it. The site is fascinating for understanding ancient Egyptian extraction techniques: you'll see tool marks, trenches carved with chisels, and traces of wooden wedges used to split the stone. Quick visit—30 to 45 minutes suffice.

Located about 13 km from Aswan, a 13-minute drive, the Aswan High Dam (Sadd el-Aali), built between 1960 and 1970 with assistance from the Soviet Union, is 3,600 meters long, 111 meters high, and 980 meters wide at its base. It created Lake Nasser, one of the world's largest artificial lakes (500 km long). The dam ended the age-old Nile floods that had governed Egyptian agriculture since the time of the pharaohs. From the top, the view takes in Lake Nasser on one side and the Nile on the other. The stop is short—20 minutes—but the perspective is impressive.

Departure at 3am from Aswan for Abu Simbel—280 km of desert road (3 to 3.5 hours), in organized convoy. Arrival at sunrise at the temples, when the raking light sets fire to the four colossi of Ramesses II. The Great Temple, carved directly into the cliff around 1265 BC, strikes with its dimensions: the facade measures 33 meters high and 38 wide. The four seated statues of Ramesses II reach 20 meters each. Inside, a hypostyle hall of eight Osirid pillars leads to the innermost sanctuary, 63 meters into the rock. Twice a year, at the equinoxes (February 22 and October 22), the sun's rays penetrate to the back of the sanctuary to illuminate three of the four seated statues—an astronomical alignment calculated 3,200 years ago.

Right next door, the Small Temple of Nefertari—one of the rare Egyptian temples dedicated to a queen—is dedicated to Nefertari and the goddess Hathor. Six 10-meter statues adorn the facade: four represent Ramesses II and two Nefertari. Inside, the wall paintings showing Nefertari crowned by the goddesses are among the best preserved in Egypt. The fact that Ramesses built a temple of this scale for his wife is unprecedented in Egyptian history.

The story of the temples' relocation is as extraordinary as the temples themselves. In 1964-1968, facing the rising waters of Lake Nasser, an unprecedented UNESCO operation cut the two temples into 1,042 blocks of 20 to 30 tons each, then reassembled them 65 meters higher and 210 meters back on an artificial hill. The total cost—financed by 50 countries—was considerable. Look carefully at the joints between blocks on the colossi: the cut lines are barely visible. Explanatory panels trace the operation behind the temples.

activities.text: Arrival in Aswan in late afternoon. The city has a slower rhythm and a more Nubian atmosphere than Luxor—the border with historical Nubia passes here. Stroll through Aswan's souk, Egypt's most colorful: spices in pyramids (cumin, saffron, henna), woven Nubian baskets, fabrics and perfumes. Vendors are less aggressive than in Cairo. The souk stretches for several hundred meters parallel to the Nile.

First felucca ride on the Nile at sunset—Aswan is where this experience is most beautiful. The river is dotted with granite islands, golden light falls on the sand dunes of the west bank, and white felucca sails glide in silence. Count on 1 to 1.5 hours. Negotiate the fare before boarding—feluccas depart from the south corniche.

Felucca crossing to Elephantine Island, in the middle of the Nile facing Aswan's corniche. The island hosts a Nubian village with brightly painted houses—blue, yellow, orange—and ruins of a temple of Khnum dating from the 30th Dynasty. The island's Nilometer, a graduated stairway plunging into the river, was used to measure the annual Nile flood and calculate taxes since pharaonic times. If you have time, push on to Kitchener Island (Aswan Botanical Garden), just next door—a tropical garden created by Lord Kitchener in the 19th century, pleasant for a shaded break.

Return to Aswan in the afternoon. Enjoy the rest of the day relaxing—after the 3am wake-up, you'll have earned it. A second felucca at sunset, iced Nubian tea (karkadé) on the corniche, or dinner at a Nubian restaurant on Elephantine Island are good options for this last evening in Aswan.

visits.text: In 1092, the vizier (head of government) Badr al-Jamali had Bab Zuweila built as one of the gates of the fortified city. Cairo was then the capital of the Fatimids, the dynasty that had founded the city in the 10th century. The two minarets atop the gate belong to the neighboring al-Mu’ayyad Mosque and date from 1415 to 1422. The gate also served as an execution site: in 1517, Tuman Bay II, the last of the Mamluk sultans who then ruled Egypt, was hanged here. It marks the southern end of al-Muizz Street, which will guide your afternoon route.

activities.text: Next, climb the spiral staircases inside the minarets of Bab Zuweila: an inexpensive ticket gives you access to the roof and towers. From above, the layout of old Cairo is much easier to understand than from the crowded street. Look out for the wooden pigeon coops on nearby rooftops, too; the birds often circle at sunset. Allow about twenty minutes, including the climb.

visits.text: Drive Cairo → Bahariya Oasis (370 km, roughly 4 hours on decent paved road). The landscape evolves gradually: Cairo's sprawl gives way to farmland, then pure desert—rocky plateau, sand stretching to infinity, no habitation for tens of kilometers. The descent into the Bahariya Depression (2,000 km²) is dramatic: the desert suddenly opens onto a green oasis of palm groves and springs.

Check into Bawiti, the oasis's main town (around 30,000 people). If you arrive by early afternoon, start with the Black Mountain (Gebel el-Ingleez, the 'English Mountain')—a WWI British observation post atop a basalt hill. The 360° view over the oasis, palm groves, and surrounding desert is Bahariya's best. Time your ascent for sunset.

The Golden Mummies Museum in Bawiti displays part of the 1996 discovery—one of the late 20th century's major archaeological finds. A Greco-Roman necropolis of over 250 mummies, some covered in remarkably preserved gilded cartonnage masks. The museum presents about a dozen in climate-controlled cases. You'll also see amulets, jewelry, and funerary pottery. The visit is brief (30-45 min) but fascinating—these mummies date from when Egypt was under Greek then Roman rule, and the mummification techniques blend pharaonic traditions with Hellenistic influences.

The nobles' tombs of Bahariya, in Bawiti village, are open to visitors—notably those of Zed-Amun-ef-Ankh and Bannentiu (26th Dynasty, around 600 BC). The well-preserved wall paintings show scenes from daily life and the journey to the afterlife. The Temple of Alexander the Great, built during his passage through the oasis in 332 BC en route to the oracle of Siwa, lies in ruins but Alexander's cartouche as pharaoh of Egypt is still visible—a rare document.

Make a stop at the salt lake and golden sand dunes on the oasis's northern edge. The lake, dry part of the year, forms a dazzling white crust that contrasts with the ochre sand and blue sky. The bordering dunes are perfect for sandboarding or simply walking barefoot in warm sand.

activities.text: Soak in one of the oasis's natural hot springs—Bir Sigam or Bir el-Ghaba ('well of the forest'), surrounded by palms. The water bubbles up at 38-45°C, rich in iron and minerals. It's total relaxation after hours on the road. The springs are open day and night—a midnight dip under the desert stars is an experience unto itself.

Lunch at a local restaurant in Bawiti—simple but authentic cooking: grilled chicken, rice, garden vegetables, wood-fired bread. In the afternoon, walk through the oasis's irrigated palm groves—an ancient network of canals distributes spring water to gardens growing dates, olives, apricots, and vegetables. The contrast between the intense green of the groves and the scorched desert surrounding them never ceases to amaze.

visits.text: Peaceful from the shore, feared by divers: Dahab’s Blue Hole is a marine sinkhole more than 100 m deep, 8 km north of town. The danger comes from the Arch, a tunnel whose ceiling lies at 55 m, beyond the 40 m limit for recreational diving. At this depth, breathing nitrogen causes a kind of intoxication that clouds judgment. The tunnel appears to be less than 10 m long; it is actually 26 m. Non-divers can take in the spectacle from the surface with a snorkeling mask on.

activities.text: Enter the water at the Bells, an entry point just north of the Blue Hole, then let the current carry you toward the sinkhole. It flows from north to south along a drop-off, a coral wall that plunges straight down. The hole itself is too deep to see the bottom: the most beautiful corals are along the drop-off. Then exit via the Blue Hole’s dock. Swim only in calm seas and stay close to the reef: accidents have happened at the surface, too.

visits.text: Arrival at Cairo International Airport (CAI). Transfer to your hotel in downtown Cairo or Giza—allow 45 minutes to 1.5 hours depending on traffic, which is legendarily chaotic in Cairo. Take time to settle in and adjust to the city's heat and noise.

If your flight arrives in early afternoon, head up the Cairo Tower on Gezira Island—187 meters tall, built in 1961, it offers the best 360° panorama of the city. On clear days, you'll spot the Giza pyramids on the horizon. The Zamalek neighborhood, on the same island, is Cairo's most pleasant district for a first stroll—colonial villas, art galleries, quiet cafés along the Nile. It's a good place to decompress before diving into Cairo's chaos.

Start with Saladin's Citadel, perched on the Mokattam heights 75 meters above the city. Built from 1176 by Saladin to defend Cairo against the Crusaders, it served as Egypt's seat of power for nearly 700 years. Inside, step into the Mosque of Muhammad Ali—nicknamed “the Alabaster Mosque” for its interior alabaster cladding rising 11 meters high. Its central dome soars to 52 meters and its Ottoman silhouette dominates Cairo's skyline. From the terrace, the view takes in all of Old Cairo, the minarets and, on clear days, the Giza pyramids on the horizon. Allow 1.5 hours on site.

Head down to the Sultan Hassan Mosque, below the Citadel—a masterpiece of Mamluk architecture. Built between 1356 and 1363 under Sultan An-Nasir Hassan, it measures 150 meters long with its southern minaret reaching 68 meters, medieval Cairo's tallest. The interior impresses with its proportions: the central courtyard opens onto four iwans (vaulted halls), each dedicated to one of the four schools of Sunni jurisprudence. Opposite, the Al-Rifai Mosque (1912) offers striking contrast—same Mamluk style but built 550 years later. It houses the tombs of Iran's last shah and several Egyptian royal family members.

Al-Azhar Mosque, founded in 970 by the Fatimids, is home to the world's second-oldest university still in operation. Its 12,000 m² combine Fatimid, Mamluk and Ottoman architectural layers - look for the three minarets, built in 1340, 1469 and 1510 respectively, each in a different style. The white marble courtyard dates from the original construction. If you are there in the late morning, you may see students attending lessons in Quranic interpretation beneath the arcades, as they have done for more than a thousand years.

If time allows, continue to Ibn Tulun Mosque (26,000 m²), built between 876 and 879. It is the oldest mosque in Cairo to have retained its original form. Its external minaret with a spiral staircase, unique in Egypt, recalls the minaret of Samarra in Iraq. Climb it for a view down into the courtyard and over Cairo's rooftops. Right next door, the Gayer-Anderson house museum (two 17th-century Ottoman houses linked by a passage) is worth a 30-minute detour.

Coptic Cairo is a neighborhood most tours neglect—wrongly. The Fortress of Babylon, built by the Romans in the 1st century, shelters within its walls the Hanging Church (Al-Moallaqa)—one of Egypt's oldest churches, its nave literally suspended above a fortress passageway. Its carved wooden ceilings and Coptic icons date from the 13th century. The Church of Saints Sergius and Bacchus (Abu Serga), below, marks the spot where, according to tradition, the Holy Family is believed to have taken refuge during their flight into Egypt. Just next door, the Ben Ezra Synagogue (9th century) is Egypt's oldest synagogue—its genizah (sacred document repository) yielded thousands of priceless medieval manuscripts discovered in the 19th century.

The National Museum of Egyptian Civilization (NMEC), opened in 2021 in the Fustat district 10 minutes from Coptic Cairo, perfectly complements the GEM. Where the GEM focuses on Pharaonic Egypt, the NMEC covers the entire story—from early humans to the 20th century, including Coptic, Islamic, and modern periods. The Royal Mummies Hall, in the basement, presents 22 pharaonic mummies (including Ramses II, Seti I, Hatshepsut) under optimal conservation conditions—soft lighting, controlled temperature, an atmosphere of reverence. The experience feels more intimate than at the GEM. Allow 2 hours.

Early departure to Saqqara, 30 km south of Cairo—the necropolis of the ancient capital Memphis. The Step Pyramid of Djoser, built around 2660 BC by the vizier Imhotep, is Egypt's oldest pyramid and humanity's first monumental stone building. Six stacked mastabas of decreasing size give it a height of 62 meters. The entrance through the colonnade—40 pillars sculpted in the shape of papyrus plants—is strikingly modern. Beneath the pyramid, a 5 km network of underground corridors descends to a depth of 28 meters to the burial chamber. You can visit part of the underground passages for an extra fee. The site is far less crowded than Giza—make the most of it.

Continue to Dahshur, 15 km south of Saqqara—an even quieter site. Here you'll see the evolution of construction techniques: the Bent Pyramid (105 meters, around 2600 BC), recognizable by its mid-height slope change—Sneferu's architects had to reduce the angle during construction to prevent collapse. Right beside it, the Red Pyramid (104 meters), history's first successful smooth-sided pyramid. It served as the direct model for Khufu's Great Pyramid. You can enter the Red Pyramid via a 63-meter corridor—the ammonia smell is strong, but the three interior chambers built of red dressed stone are worth seeing.

Make a detour to the Imhotep Museum at Saqqara before leaving—small but remarkable. The blue faience tiles recovered from inside Djoser's pyramid, the mummy of Merenre I, and Imhotep's wooden coffin are displayed here. It's a useful addition to a visit to the necropolis, helping you understand it.

Morning flight Aswan → Cairo (1 hour 15 minutes). Final free day in Cairo for shopping, revisiting a favorite site, or simply wandering. Zamalek is pleasant for a last stroll—art galleries, cafés, boutiques. Khan el-Khalili souk is also a good spot for last-minute gifts if you didn't have time on Day 2.

activities.text: First Egyptian dinner in Zamalek or along the Nile Corniche. Egyptian street food is worth trying on your very first evening: koshari (lentils, rice, pasta, spicy tomato sauce—the national dish), ful medames (stewed fava beans), ta'ameya (falafel made from fava beans). Corniche restaurants offer views of the illuminated Nile—a good introduction.

Plunge into Khan el-Khalili souk, founded in 1382 by Emir Djaharks al-Khalili on the former burial ground of Fatimid caliphs. Over 900 shops crowd into a labyrinth of covered alleys—goldsmiths, spice vendors, hammered copper, perfumes. Walk up Al-Muizz Street, one of Cairo's oldest (10th century), lined with 29 UNESCO-listed Islamic monuments. Don't miss mint tea at El-Fishawy café, open continuously since 1773. The souk hits its stride late afternoon when the heat breaks and the alleys come alive.

Dinner in Old Cairo—Egyptian street food is worth trying: koshari (lentils, rice, pasta and spicy tomato sauce), ful medames (stewed fava beans), ta'ameya (Egyptian falafel made from fava beans rather than chickpeas). The hole-in-the-wall joints around Khan el-Khalili serve generous portions. For a more relaxed experience, several restaurants with terraces overlook Al-Hussein Square.

Walk through the Fustat district, Cairo's oldest neighborhood (founded in 641 by Arab conquerors, even before the Fatimid founding of Cairo in 969). Al-Azhar Park, created in 2005 on a former 30-hectare garbage dump, offers panoramic views of the old city and its minarets—one of Cairo's rare green spaces. A good place for a breather in a packed day.

Stop at Memphis, the ancient capital of the Old Kingdom, 3 km north of Saqqara. The Mit Rahinah open-air museum displays the reclining colossus of Ramses II (10 meters long, in limestone) and an alabaster sphinx weighing 80 tonnes from the New Kingdom. Memphis was founded around 3100 BC by Menes (Narmer), the pharaoh who unified Upper and Lower Egypt—it remained the capital for over a thousand years. Today, almost nothing remains of the city itself, swallowed by groundwater and modern construction. The museum takes 30 to 45 minutes to visit.
Transfer to Cairo International Airport (CAI) for your return flight. The airport is 30-45 minutes from downtown—allow extra time due to traffic.

visits.text: On its rocky promontory in the Moqattam Hills, the Citadel of Saladin has towered over Cairo for more than eight centuries. Saladin began construction in the 1170s, and the site remained the seat of Egyptian power for nearly 700 years. From a distance, however, the most prominent features are the domes and minarets of a more recent mosque, that of Muhammad Ali, Egypt’s ruler in the 19th century. It was built from 1832 to 1857, modeled on the mosques of Istanbul. Cover your shoulders and knees and remove your shoes; a headscarf is recommended for women.

Around 1846, Louis-Philippe, King of the French, gave Muhammad Ali the clock that adorns the citadel’s mosque. It was a gift in return for the Luxor Obelisk, which now stands in Place de la Concorde in Paris. The clock remained out of order for a long time, until it was repaired under King Farouk. From the citadel, the view stretches across Cairo and the City of the Dead, a cemetery where sultans are buried and families without homes now live.

visits.text: The Masbat promenade follows the seafront in northern Dahab, lined with cafés and beach restaurants. To the south lie the neighborhoods of Mashraba, followed by Medina. The city’s name, Dahab, means “gold” in Arabic. Bedouin children go from table to table selling woven bracelets. Choose a seaside terrace for dinner, and keep some small change for these purchases.

End the day in Assala, the predominantly Bedouin neighborhood in northern Dahab, beyond the Masbat promenade. In 1980, Dahab had fewer than 30 Bedouin families, who lived off fishing and their goats. Today, Assala remains the neighborhood where most Bedouins live, alongside Egyptians and a few foreigners. Fruits and vegetables cost much less here than along the waterfront: stock up for the next day’s drive.

activities.text: Colorful sails skim across the flat water as soon as the wind picks up over Dahab’s lagoon. The city is renowned worldwide for windsurfing. The Gulf of Aqaba acts as a corridor that funnels the wind. The lagoon is shallow enough to stand in almost everywhere, allowing instructors to stay close to beginners. The windiest months run from March through November.

Slip into the water at Lighthouse Reef, in Ghazala Bay, right in central Dahab. Entry is from the beach, and a shallow shelf borders the reef, allowing swimmers of all levels to swim above the corals. You will encounter giant pufferfish, blue-spotted rays, and, with a little luck, a turtle. Farther out, a seagrass meadow sometimes attracts seahorses. Enter and exit over the sand so you never step on the coral.

If the sea is calm, head to Eel Garden via a narrow street signposted from Dahab’s promenade. The city’s largest colony of garden eels lives on the sandy bottom. These slender fish disappear into their burrows as you approach, then reappear if you remain still. Eagle rays often glide above the sand. Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon for softer underwater light.

visits.text: Wake on the Nile—the boat sailed overnight from Luxor and passes through the Esna lock in the early morning (sometimes with a wait of 1–2 hours depending on river traffic). Arrival at Edfu mid-morning. The Temple of Edfu, dedicated to the falcon god Horus, is the best-preserved Ptolemaic temple in Egypt—and the second largest after Karnak. Built between 237 and 57 BC, it took 180 years to complete. Its entrance pylon rises 36 meters high with reliefs showing Ptolemy XII smiting his enemies before Horus. Inside, the hypostyle hall with 18 columns is intact, with its ceiling still in place—extremely rare in Egypt. The gray granite naos of the sanctuary, which housed Horus's statue, remains in place. Allow 1 to 1.5 hours for the visit.

activities.text: Afternoon sailing on the Nile between Edfu and Kom Ombo. The cruise passes through a landscape of palm groves, sugarcane fields and Nubian villages on both banks. This is the moment to enjoy the boat's upper deck—tea, reading, birdwatching (herons, egrets, kingfishers). The late afternoon light on the Nile is extraordinary for photography.

visits.text: In the heart of Coptic Cairo, the historic Christian quarter, al-Muallaqa Church takes its name from its position. This Arabic word means “the hanging one”: its nave sits above a gate of the ancient Roman Fortress of Babylon and spans a passageway. You reach it by climbing 29 steps. In 1047, it became the residence of the Coptic pope, head of Egypt’s Christian Church, when the seat moved from Alexandria. Inside, look for the icons: the church has 110, the oldest dating to the 8th century.

visits.text: The main attraction at the El Alamein Military Museum is its courtyard, where tanks and artillery still bear the marks of combat. Two battles took place here: the first in July 1942, the second from October 23 to November 4, 1942. They pitted Commonwealth troops, from the United Kingdom and the countries of its former empire, against the German and Italian armies. Inside, a room for each country displays uniforms, maps, and weapons: the Commonwealth, Germany, Italy, and Egypt. Arrive when it opens in the morning, before the heat sets in.

The silence is the first thing that strikes you at El Alamein War Cemetery, where Commonwealth soldiers are buried. More than 7,200 graves stand in rows, including those of 815 soldiers who were never identified. The cemetery memorial also bears the names of 11,866 service members with no known grave. Field Marshal Montgomery, the victor of the second battle, inaugurated it in 1954. Take time to read the ages engraved on the headstones.

Continue west to the German Memorial at El Alamein, beside the coastal road to Marsa Matrouh. This octagonal building, with a tower at each corner, resembles a fortified castle: Germans call this type of monument a Totenburg, or “castle of the dead.” Inaugurated in 1959, it houses the remains of about 4,300 soldiers. Stay on roads and designated paths: France Diplomatie warns of the risk of mines in desert areas.

IGNOTO, Italian for “unknown”: this word appears on many graves at the Italian Memorial at El Alamein. More than 4,800 Italian soldiers are buried here. Paolo Caccia Dominioni, an engineer and veteran of the battle, designed the memorial. A small museum at the entrance displays maps, artillery, and photographs. Stop here on your way back from Marsa Matrouh: the site stands beside the coastal road, west of El Alamein.

visits.text: The trip's most spectacular day—by 4x4 with a Bedouin guide. Depart Bahariya heading south. First stop: the Black Desert (Sahara el-Suda), a lunar landscape of volcanic hills blanketed in basalt fragments—you could be on another planet. The black stones crunch underfoot and conical mounds march across the horizon. Your guide leads you up one of the hills for a panoramic view of this surreal terrain.

Continue to Crystal Mountain—a rocky outcrop encrusted with quartz and calcite crystals that sparkle in the sun. It's not really a mountain but a ridge a few meters high, sitting in the middle of nowhere. Further on, Agabat Valley offers white rock formations sculpted by wind amid golden dunes—one of the Western Desert's most photographed landscapes.

The White Desert (Sahara el-Beyda) is the trip's highlight. White limestone formations, sculpted by millennia of wind erosion, rise like giant mushrooms, columns, animal heads—an open-air museum of natural sculptures. The white rock, which was once the bed of the Tethys Sea 50 million years ago, contrasts violently with golden sand and deep blue sky. At sunset, the formations shift from white to pink to orange—the spectacle is hypnotic.

Wake at sunrise in the White Desert—the low morning light gives the limestone formations long shadows and golden hues. It's the best time for photography. Bedouin breakfast at camp (bread, cheese, jam, tea), then a morning hike through the formations. Your guide will show you fossils of shells and coral embedded in the limestone—reminders that this area was a seabed millions of years ago.

Drive to Farafra Oasis (90 km south of the White Desert), the smallest and most isolated of the Western Desert's major oases—around 5,000 people. Farafra's old village, at the foot of a hill, preserves its traditional mud-brick architecture. The atmosphere is peaceful, almost timeless. Visit the small local museum and the palm groves irrigated by natural springs.

activities.text: Camp in the White Desert—your Bedouin guide sets up camp among the limestone formations, prepares a wood-fire dinner (grilled chicken, rice, vegetables, mint tea), and you sleep under the stars or in a tent. With zero light pollution, the desert's starry sky is more intense than you've probably ever seen—the Milky Way is visible to the naked eye from horizon to horizon. The silence is absolute. It's one of the trip's most memorable nights.

Swim at Bir Setta hot springs (spring #6), a few kilometers from Farafra—sulfurous water at 38°C, surrounded by palms. It's travelers' favorite relaxation spot after days of 4x4 in the desert. In the afternoon, enjoy the oasis's calm or explore the irrigated gardens growing dates, olives, and apricots.

visits.text: Long drive from Farafra to Fayoum Oasis (around 484 km, 6 hours 10 minutes via the desert road and El Haiz). The landscape is monotonous but grand—desert plateau as far as the eye can see, then a gradual descent into the Fayoum Depression. Arrival in the oasis, with its lakes, palm groves, and cultivated fields, is a welcome relief after two days in the desert.

The village of Tunis, perched on a hill above Lake Qarun, lies west of the town of Fayoum: allow for the drive from your overnight town. It has become a center of ceramic craftsmanship. Several pottery workshops are open to visitors - you can watch the potters at work or try the wheel yourself. The terraces of the village's cafés and lodges offer a panoramic view over Lake Qarun. In winter, flamingos and other migratory birds gather there.

Wadi al-Hitan - the Valley of the Whales, a UNESCO site since 2005, lies deep in the desert west of the town of Fayoum, beyond the Wadi el-Rayan lakes. Allow a full-day round trip from your overnight town, with the last part of the journey by 4x4 on a desert track. This open-air museum holds the fossil skeletons of primitive whales 40 million years old. The largest skeleton found - a Basilosaurus - is 21 meters long, with five-fingered front flippers and hind legs still visible. These fossils are direct proof that whales descend from land mammals. A small modern museum traces the history of the discoveries with an explanatory video. The site can only be explored on foot along marked trails - vehicles are banned from the fossil zone.

On the way back, stop at the Wadi el-Rayan waterfalls—Egypt's only waterfall, formed by flow between two artificial lakes. The flow is modest but the contrast between falling water and surrounding desert is striking. It's a good picnic stop.

activities.text: Sunset over Lake Qarun from Tunis village—the sky's colors reflect in the lake, with silhouettes of palms in the foreground. It's a moment of absolute calm after days of desert adventure. Dinner at one of the village lodges—simple, fresh Egyptian cooking.

Last afternoon in Fayoum—stroll through the irrigated palm groves, visit a traditional water wheel (sakieh), birdwatch at Lake Qarun if the season's right. Fayoum is rural Egypt condensed—far from crowds, authentic, peaceful. It's the perfect counterpoint to the desert days.

visits.text: The Grand Egyptian Museum (GEM), inaugurated November 1, 2025, is the world's largest archaeological museum dedicated to a single civilization—500,000 square meters total area, 100,000 objects displayed across 12 permanent halls covering seven millennia of history. It sits 2 km from the pyramids on the Giza plateau. Right at the entrance, the colossal statue of Ramesses II (11 meters, 83 tons, 3,200 years old) welcomes you in the atrium. The Grand Staircase, spanning six levels and 6,000 square meters, is lined with some sixty monumental statues with direct views of the pyramids through the glass facade. The complete Tutankhamun collection—5,398 pieces, many displayed for the first time—occupies 7,500 square meters alone. Count on a minimum of 4 hours, ideally 6 for a complete visit. Tickets are no longer sold on-site—book online.

After the museum, head to the Giza plateau 2 km away—a pedestrian bridge now connects the two sites. The Pyramid of Khufu, sole survivor of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, has stood for more than 4,500 years. The numbers are dizzying: 230 meters per side, 146 meters tall originally (138 today), 2.3 million limestone blocks averaging 2.5 tons each, for a total weight of 5 million tons. It was the world's tallest building for 3,800 years. If you go inside (extra fee), expect a narrow, steep corridor leading to the King's Chamber—10.5 m by 5.2 m in solid granite. It's physical and claustrophobic, but the experience is worth it. Arrive at opening (8am) to avoid crowds and heat.

The Sphinx, carved directly from a rocky outcrop on the plateau, measures 73.5 meters long and 20 meters high—the largest carved monolith from antiquity. Its face, probably that of Pharaoh Khafre (4th Dynasty, around 2500 BC), looks due east toward the sunrise. Don't miss the Panoramic Point (Nine Pyramids viewpoint) on the road that curves around the southern plateau—this is where you'll get all three great pyramids and the three smaller queens' pyramids aligned in a single frame.

activities.text: Sunset over the pyramids from the Panoramic Point or from one of the terrace restaurants on Fayoum Road that runs along the plateau. The golden light on the pyramids in late afternoon is the best photographic moment—tour buses have left and the heat is bearable. Some organize camel or horse rides around the plateau in late afternoon.

visits.text: Look up as soon as you enter the Grand Egyptian Museum’s main hall: a statue of Ramesses II, 11 m tall and weighing 83 tonnes, welcomes visitors. It stood in Ramses Square in Cairo until it was moved in 2006. The museum, which officially opened on November 1, 2025, is 2 km from the pyramids. Book online: tickets are sold for a specific day and time slot, and are no longer available at the ticket counter.

Next, take your time climbing the Grand Staircase at the GEM, the museum’s English acronym. Its 148 steps are lined with more than 60 ancient artifacts, displayed as in a gallery. At the top, the view stretches to the pyramids you have just left. A moving walkway runs alongside the steps for those who prefer to skip the climb, and a platform accommodates wheelchairs.

For the first time, all 5,398 objects found in Tutankhamun’s tomb are displayed together in his dedicated galleries at the Grand Egyptian Museum. The route follows five sections, from the discovery of the tomb to the king’s life and funeral. The museum suggests a 2-hour tour of these galleries, and that is a minimum. Only cell phone photography is allowed here: leave your camera in your bag.

If you have 1 hour left, finish at the Khufu Boats Museum within the Grand Egyptian Museum. These two boats, about 4,600 years old, are among the oldest wooden vessels ever discovered. They were moved here in August 2021 from the former boat museum on the Giza Plateau. On Wednesdays and Saturdays, the GEM stays open until 9 PM instead of 6 PM, giving you more time on those two days.

visits.text: Start with the Great Pyramid of Khufu, the tallest of the Pyramids of Giza. It stood 146.6 m tall around 2600 BC and now measures only 138.5 m. Its white limestone casing was removed over the centuries, leaving the inner blocks visible today. About 2.3 million blocks were needed. It is the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and the only one to remain almost intact. The plateau opens at 7 AM: arrive early, before the heat and the tour groups.

activities.text: If tight spaces don’t bother you, buy the separate ticket to enter the Pyramid of Khufu. A corridor leads to the Grand Gallery, a sloping passage 46.7 m long and 8.6 m high. At the end, the King’s Chamber contains only a granite sarcophagus. This ticket cost 1,500 Egyptian pounds in 2026, more than twice the site admission fee (700 pounds): book it if you really want to see the interior.

visits.text: Flight Aswan → Hurghada (1 hour) or transfer by road (about 495 km, 7 hours' drive through the Eastern Desert). Arrival on the Red Sea coast—the contrast with the Nile valley is dramatic: here it's turquoise blue as far as the eye can see, coral reefs and the desert plunging into the sea. Check-in at the hotel and first swim. The Red Sea water is 24–28°C all year round, with visibility that often exceeds 30 meters.

Boat excursion to the Giftun Islands—a marine national park 45 minutes by boat from Hurghada. The two islands (Giftun Kebir and Giftun Soraya) are surrounded by some of the northern Red Sea's most beautiful coral reefs. The water is turquoise and crystal clear, the white sand beaches nearly deserted. Snorkeling here is exceptional: parrotfish, Napoleon wrasses, butterflyfish, stingrays, and with luck green sea turtles. Multiple snorkeling stops are planned at different reefs throughout the day.

Last day in Hurghada—several options depending on your interests. For underwater enthusiasts: an introductory scuba dive (no experience required, full supervision, 1.5 hours total) lets you descend to 6–10 meters on a reef—an experience unlike surface snorkeling. The reefs around Giftun and Abu Ramada are perfect for a first dive, with weak currents and exceptional visibility.

Last morning in Hurghada. If your flight is late in the day, enjoy a final swim or early morning snorkel on the hotel reef. Hurghada International Airport (HRG) is 10–15 minutes from downtown—far simpler than Cairo. Direct flights to Paris, Lyon, Brussels, Geneva and most European capitals, as well as connections via Cairo.

activities.text: A day to unwind after 10 days of intensive sightseeing. Enjoy your hotel beach or head down to Hurghada marina for a walk—restaurants, cafés and shops line the port. If you still have energy, take a stroll through the old El Dahar quarter to discover authentic Hurghada—local souk, mosques, neighborhood life far from the resorts.

First snorkeling session from the beach—most Hurghada hotels have a reef accessible directly from shore or from a jetty. The Red Sea harbors over 800 fish species and 200 coral species. Even from the beach, you'll see butterflyfish, clownfish, surgeonfish and probably a moray eel or two.

Full day at sea with lunch on board. Excursions typically include 2 to 3 snorkeling stops at different reefs—gardens of hard and soft corals, drop-offs, shallow lagoons. The natural lagoon of Giftun Soraya, with waters 0.5–1.5 meters deep, is perfect for beginners and families. The reefs on the south side offer more spectacular drop-offs for experienced snorkelers. Return to Hurghada late afternoon.

Alternative: excursion to Dolphin Reef (Sha'ab el-Erg), about 1.5 hours by boat north of Hurghada. A pod of spinner dolphins permanently resides in the area—chances of sighting are high, especially in the morning. Swimming in open water near the dolphins (without touching or feeding them), then snorkeling on surrounding reefs.

Late afternoon relaxation at the beach or hotel pool. Last sunset over the Red Sea from the marina. Hurghada is also known for its Eastern Desert excursions (quad biking, 4x4 safari, Bedouin dinner)—an option if you want to mix things up for this last evening.

Transfer to Hurghada Airport (HRG) for your return flight. The airport is small and quick to get through—arriving 1.5 hours before departure is enough for international flights. If you're returning via Cairo, allow plenty of time for your connection (3 hours minimum) to accommodate any potential delay.

activities.text: Khan el-Khalili emerged in the late 14th century around a khan, a merchants’ inn built around a courtyard where goods were stored. The emir (high-ranking dignitary) Jaharkas al-Khalili, master of Sultan Barquq’s stables, had it built. Today, its shops sell souvenirs, antiques, and jewelry, and the neighboring goldsmiths’ souk remains popular with Cairo residents. Enter through the Bab al-Badistan gate, built around 1511, and save this stroll for the end of the day.

The best part of Khan el-Khalili is enjoyed sitting down at El Fishawy café, which opened in 1773 in an alley of the souk. It is one of the market’s oldest and best-known cafés. Egyptian writer Naguib Mahfouz set one of his novels, published in 1947, in an alley in Khan el-Khalili. Take a seat in the passageway, order some tea, and watch the neighborhood go by: it is the ideal way to end your stay.

places.name: Luxor

visits.text: Early-morning departure for Saqqara, 30 km south of Cairo—the necropolis of the ancient capital Memphis. The step pyramid of Djoser, built around 2660 BC by the vizier Imhotep, is the oldest pyramid in Egypt. Six stacked mastabas of decreasing size give it a height of 62 meters. The entrance through the colonnade—40 pillars carved in the shape of papyrus—is striking in its modernity. Beneath the pyramid, a 5 km network of underground corridors descends to a depth of 28 meters to reach the burial chamber. It is possible to visit part of the underground passages for an extra fee. The site is far less crowded than Giza—make the most of it.

Continue to Dahshur, 15 km south of Saqqara—an even quieter site. Here you'll see the evolution of construction techniques: the Bent Pyramid (105 meters, circa 2600 BC), recognizable by its mid-height slope change—Sneferu's architects had to reduce the angle mid-construction to prevent collapse. Right next door, the Red Pyramid (104 meters), the first successful smooth-sided pyramid in history. It served as the direct model for Khufu's Great Pyramid. You can enter the Red Pyramid through a 63-meter corridor—the ammonia smell is strong, but the three interior chambers built of dressed red stone are worth the visit.

Stop by the Imhotep Museum at Saqqara before leaving—small but remarkable. The blue faience tiles found inside Djoser's pyramid, Merenre I's mummy, and Imhotep's wooden coffin are on display. It's a good way to deepen your understanding of the necropolis.

Karnak brings together more than 2 km² of temples, pylons, obelisks and sanctuaries built over 2,000 years by dozens of pharaohs, from Senusret I (around 2000 BC) to the Ptolemies. Arrive at opening time (6 a.m.) to have the Great Hypostyle Hall almost to yourself. This forest of 134 columns, built by Seti I and completed by Ramses II, measures 103 meters long by 52 meters wide—it could contain Notre-Dame de Paris. The 12 central columns rise to 23 meters, with capitals 3.5 meters in diameter. In the low-angled morning light, the reliefs carved in the stone stand out strikingly. Allow at least 2.5 hours for Karnak, 3 hours if you want to explore its nooks and crannies.

Don't leave Karnak without circling the sacred lake (120 × 77 meters), where priests purified themselves before ceremonies. The obelisk of Hatshepsut, the tallest still standing in Egypt (29 meters, carved from a single block of Aswan pink granite), rises between the 4th and 5th pylons. At the end of the main axis, the sanctuary of Amun's barque—the temple's spiritual heart—contains remarkably well-preserved wall paintings. At the entrance, 40 ram-headed sphinxes (criosphinxes) line the processional avenue that once led to the Nile.

The Luxor Museum, on the Nile corniche between Karnak and Luxor temples, is a small, remarkably well-designed museum—far more pleasant than Cairo's old museum. Among the major pieces: two royal mummies (Ahmose I and Ramses I), a colossal granite head of Amenhotep III, and the talatat wall—283 painted sandstone blocks from the Temple of Aten that Akhenaten had built at Karnak before his successors demolished it. Allow 1 to 1.5 hours.

Wake at 4:30 a.m. for a hot air balloon flight over the west bank—one of Egypt's most spectacular experiences. The balloon lifts off at sunrise and soars over the Valley of the Kings, Hatshepsut's temple and the sugarcane fields along the Nile for 45 minutes to 1 hour. Reservations are made the day before—flights are canceled in high winds.

The Valley of the Kings holds 63 tombs carved into the rock between 1539 and 1075 BC—New Kingdom pharaohs had abandoned pyramids in favor of underground tombs to escape looters. Your ticket includes 3 tombs of your choice. The most impressive for their paintings: Ramses IV (KV2), Ramses IX (KV6), Merenptah (KV8). Seti I's tomb (KV17), considered the valley's most beautiful, requires a substantial supplement. Tutankhamun's tomb (KV62), discovered in 1922 by Howard Carter, is small and its paintings less spectacular than others—the 5,398 objects of the treasure are now at the GEM in Giza. Arrive before 7am—there's no shade in the valley and the heat quickly becomes unbearable.

The Colossi of Memnon, two seated statues of Amenhotep III standing 18 meters tall each, guard the entrance to what was Luxor's largest mortuary temple—now vanished. They were carved from quartzite blocks weighing 720 tonnes each, transported from the Gebel el-Ahmar quarries near Cairo, 675 km away. In antiquity, the northern colossus emitted a sound at sunrise (probably due to expansion of stone cracked by an earthquake in 27 BC)—Greeks and Romans came from afar to hear it. The stop is quick—15 to 20 minutes suffice.

Hatshepsut's mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari stands against a 300-meter cliff that serves as its natural backdrop—the architectural spectacle is unique in Egypt. Three monumental terraces connected by ramps rise against the rock face. The first measures 120 meters deep by 75 wide. The temple, built in 15 years by architect Senenmut, depicts on its walls the trade expedition to the land of Punt (present-day Somalia/Eritrea)—you can see the frankincense trees transported by boat—and the divine birth of the queen. Hatshepsut, the only woman to have reigned as pharaoh for 22 years, had most of her depictions chiseled away by her successor Thutmose III after her death in 1458 BC. Arrive early—the temple is in full sun from 9 a.m.

Continue to Medinet Habu—Ramses III's mortuary temple, less crowded than Karnak but whose painted reliefs are the best preserved on the entire west bank. The battle scenes against the Sea Peoples (circa 1178 BC) still retain their original colors—blue, red, yellow. The ceiling of the second portico preserves traces of vivid pigments after 3,000 years. The outer enclosure, inspired by a Syrian fortress (the Migdol), is unique in Egyptian temple architecture. If you only see one 'off-the-beaten-path' temple in Luxor, this is the one.

The Ramesseum, Ramses II's mortuary temple, is worth a stop for its monumental remains—notably a broken colossus of Ramses II that weighed over 1,000 tonnes and measured about 18 meters when standing. This is the colossus that inspired Shelley's poem Ozymandias in 1818. The hypostyle hall still retains part of its ceiling with astronomical paintings. The site is less restored than Karnak, giving it the charm of a romantic ruin.

activities.text: Cairo → Luxor flight in late afternoon (1-hour flight, several airlines offer daily departures). Upon arrival, settle on the east bank of the Nile. If your flight arrives before sunset, head straight to Luxor Temple—it's magnificent at night, illuminated. The pylon of Ramses II, his two seated colossi of 15 meters, and the remaining obelisk (the second has been in Paris's Place de la Concorde since 1836) form the entrance. Amenhotep III's processional colonnade, 20 meters high, gives you chills under the spotlights. The avenue of human-headed sphinxes, restored and reopened in 2021 after decades of work, connects Luxor Temple to Karnak over 2.7 km—you can walk along it in the cool evening air.

Late afternoon stroll along the Nile corniche between Luxor Temple and downtown. Luxor's east bank comes alive at sunset—feluccas glide on the river, restaurant terraces light up. If you haven't yet seen Karnak by night, the sound and light show (nightly, multiple languages) takes you through the illuminated temple—it's kitschy but the atmosphere in the hypostyle hall under the spotlights is worth it.

Free afternoon to recover from the 4:30am wake-up. If you still have energy, detour to Deir el-Medina, the village of artisans who built and decorated the Valley of the Kings tombs for 500 years. The small workers' tombs—notably those of Sennedjem and Inherkhau—are paradoxically better painted than some royal tombs, with colors of astonishing freshness. The site is little visited and gives insight into the daily life of the royal tomb builders.

The Valley of the Queens holds around a hundred tombs of royal wives and children, three of which can generally be visited with the standard ticket: Titi (QV52), Khaemwaset (QV44) and Amunherkhepeshef (QV55), the latter two sons of Ramses III. Their brightly colored paintings show the pharaoh presenting the young prince to the gods. The tomb of Nefertari (QV66), considered the most beautiful tomb in all of Egypt for the vividness of its wall paintings, has been closed since March 2024 for restoration, with no reopening date announced—check on site whether it has reopened. The site is noticeably quieter than the Valley of the Kings.

Board the cruise boat moored at Luxor in the late afternoon. Settle into your cabin and enjoy your first dinner on board facing the sunset over the Nile. The Luxor-Aswan cruise lasts 2 nights and 3 days, with stops at Edfu and Kom Ombo. The boat sails mainly at night—you fall asleep at one stop and wake at the next.

visits.text: During part of the El Alamein campaign in 1942, German Field Marshal Erwin Rommel established his headquarters in caves in Marsa Matrouh. Since 1977, they have housed the Rommel Museum on the peninsula bordering the harbor to the east. His son Manfred donated several items: his leather coat, binoculars, compass, and maps with his handwritten annotations. Reopened in 2017 after restoration, the museum can be visited in less than 1 hour.

activities.text: You’ll spend the afternoon at Rommel Beach, just past the museum at the tip of Marsa Matrouh’s eastern peninsula. The calm but rocky shoreline is well suited to swimming. The sea is warmest from June to October: an average of 23 to 26 °C in Alexandria, farther east along the same coast. Bring water shoes for the rocks, and return to town before nightfall.

visits.text: Al-Azhar Mosque was the first mosque founded in the city nicknamed “the city of a thousand minarets.” The Fatimids built it between 970 and 972 for their new capital. Students often relax in its courtyard, paved with white marble. Remove your shoes; women must cover their arms, legs, and hair, with a scarf available to borrow at the entrance. Avoid Friday prayers.

visits.text: Right next door, al-Rifai Mosque resembles its medieval neighbor, but it was only completed in 1912. Commissioned for the mother of Khedive Ismail, Egypt’s ruler in the 19th century, it was intended to rival the Mosque of Sultan Hassan in grandeur and height. It houses the tombs of the Egyptian royal family, including those of Kings Fuad I and Farouk. Iran’s last shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, who died in Cairo in 1980, is also buried here. Twenty minutes is enough.

visits.text: You feel tiny at the foot of the 38 m entrance portal of the Mosque-Madrasa of Sultan Hassan. A madrasa is a religious school. Here, four iwans, large vaulted halls opening onto the courtyard, each housed one of the four schools of Sunni Islamic law. Construction, from 1356 to 1363, was partly funded by the estates of emirs, high-ranking officers who had died of the plague and whose wealth reverted to the treasury. Assassinated in 1361, the sultan was never laid to rest in his mausoleum: his body was never found. Come in the morning for the light.

visits.text: The cold stings your fingers at the summit of Mount Sinai, at 2,285 m, as the sky grows pale behind the ridges. Arabs call it Jebel Musa, the Mountain of Moses. Tradition holds that Moses received the Tablets of the Law here, making it sacred to Christians, Muslims, and Jews. An Orthodox chapel built in 1934, which is closed to visitors, replaces a 16th-century church. Arrive before dawn to find an east-facing spot.

activities.text: To watch the sunrise from Mount Sinai, set out after midnight with a headlamp. The Camel Path begins behind Saint Catherine’s Monastery: wide and gently sloping, it takes about 2 hours 30 minutes to walk. Camels wait at the start to carry the most tired hikers much of the way up. A Bedouin guide is required; you can find one at the monastery parking lot. Even in summer, it is cold and windy at the top: bring a warm jacket and water.

Descend via the Steps of Repentance, a stone staircase built in the 6th century and the steepest route to the monastery. The staircase has 3,750 steps: 750 between the summit and Elijah’s Basin, then about 3,000 to the bottom. Elijah’s Basin is a small plateau about 300 m below the summit, where a 500-year-old cypress grows. The steps are high and uneven: wear footwear with good ankle support. Descend slowly to reach the monastery around its opening time, at 9 a.m.

visits.text: The Egyptian Museum in Cairo has lost Tutankhamun and its royal mummies, yet it remains a major attraction. Tutankhamun’s artifacts moved to the Grand Egyptian Museum, and 22 mummies went to the Museum of Egyptian Civilization in 2021. The building, which opened in 1902 near Tahrir Square, remains filled with statues and sarcophagi. The museum is open from 9 AM to 5 PM, but the ticket office closes at 4 PM and accepts payment by card only.

Start by looking for the Narmer Palette at the Egyptian Museum in Cairo. This stone slab, carved around 3100 BC, depicts King Narmer. It is often described as the oldest Egyptian historical document. Continue with the colossal statues of Pharaoh Amenhotep III and his wife Tiye. Also look for the sphinx with the face of Queen Hatshepsut, whose mummy you saw a few hours earlier. Allow at least 1 hour for these galleries.

visits.text: On April 3, 2021, 22 royal mummies traveled through Cairo in a procession from the Egyptian Museum on Tahrir Square. This procession, the Pharaohs’ Golden Parade, marked the inauguration of the National Museum of Egyptian Civilization. The 18 kings and 4 queens, including Hatshepsut, now rest in the Royal Mummies Hall, designed to evoke the Valley of the Kings, where the pharaohs were buried. The museum is open from 9 AM to 5 PM, with last admission at 4 PM.

The main gallery at the Museum of Egyptian Civilization deserves more than a quick walk through on your way to the mummies. It traces Egypt’s history from prehistoric to modern times, covering the pharaonic, Greco-Roman, Coptic, and Islamic periods. A separate gallery displays around 600 Egyptian textiles. On Fridays, there is a second evening session from 6 PM to 9 PM if your day is too full.

visits.text: Nabq is home to the northernmost mangrove forest in the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean. Established in 1992, the reserve covers 600 km² north of Sharm el-Sheikh. Its mangrove trees, which grow in salt water, form an almost continuous fringe stretching 4.5 km along the shore. Stay on marked tracks: the French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs warns that the risk of land mines is high off roads in desert areas.

activities.text: Twisted metal sheets resting on the reef about a hundred meters offshore: this is the wreck of the Maria Schröder in the Nabq reserve. Built in Norway in 1920, this cargo ship ran aground on April 11, 1956, while sailing from Aqaba to West Germany. Part of the wreck rests on the reef flat. The rest lies scattered at depths of up to 24 m. When snorkeling, stay above the shallow sections and wear water shoes when entering the water to avoid damaging the coral.

visits.text: The Pyramid of Khafre looks taller than the Pyramid of Khufu, yet it is smaller. The explanation lies in the terrain: it stands on a rocky base 10 m higher. Look up at its summit: the upper third still retains some of its original casing. This remnant shows what the pyramids looked like when they were built: smooth faces with no visible steps. The plateau’s free shuttle stops at its base if you find the walk tiring.

visits.text: In 1196, al-Aziz Uthman, son of Sultan Saladin, set out to demolish the pyramids, starting with the Pyramid of Menkaure. The damage is limited to a large vertical gash in the north face. It is the smallest of the three great Pyramids of Giza, originally 65 m tall and now 61 m. At its base, seven courses of granite casing remain in place. Walk around to the north face to see the gash.

activities.text: Next, take the shuttle to the Panorama overlook, the designated viewpoint on the Giza Plateau. From here, you can take in the pyramids at a glance, with the desert behind them: this is the spot for a photo of the entire site. Touts offer camel rides and posed photos here. Decline with “La shukran” (“no thank you” in Arabic), or agree on the price before getting on.

visits.text: The best moment at Ras Abu Galum may be spent under a Bedouin hut with a glass of tea in hand. The Bedouins of the Mizena tribe make their living here from small-scale fishing, which is now regulated. Their rustic camps serve meals and rent out a few huts for overnight stays facing the Gulf of Aqaba. Before settling in, book your return boat to the Blue Hole: departures do not follow a fixed schedule.

activities.text: You can reach Ras Abu Galum from the Blue Hole on foot, by camel, or by boat, and that is its charm. Protected since 1992, the reserve covers about 500 km² where granite mountains meet the Gulf of Aqaba. The coastal trail takes about 1 hour 30 minutes on foot. Once there, walk 500 to 800 m along the shore: the corals are more beautiful in the coves than off the main beach. Bring your mask and plenty of water.

visits.text: A long crack cuts through the desert floor, with still water far below: these are the earthquake fissures in Ras Mohammed National Park. They opened during seismic tremors, about 150 m from the sea. The longest measures nearly 40 m, with a width ranging from 20 cm to 1.5 m. Some pools are more than 14 m deep. Look from the edge without leaning over: the rock can slip beneath your feet.

The Bedouins regarded Ras Mohammed’s Magic Lake as a wishing lake. According to their legend, people would throw a precious stone into it while making a wish, and these gems are said to carpet the bottom. The scientific explanation is simpler: the water changes color with the sun’s position, several times a day. The water in this small lake is also very salty, so you float effortlessly. Stop by twice, in the late morning and again in the late afternoon, to compare the colors.

The mangrove channel is the most peaceful spot in Ras Mohammed. At the tip of the park, about 0.9 hectares of mangrove trees line a shallow channel 1.16 km long. Mangrove trees grow with their feet in seawater. Their roots shelter young fish and small crustaceans as they grow. Walk slowly along the bank and watch the water between the roots, where fry, or very young fish, hide.

activities.text: More than 1,000 fish species inhabit the reefs of Ras Mohammed National Park, which has been protected since 1983. The park occupies the southern tip of Sinai, between the Gulf of Suez to the west and the Gulf of Aqaba to the east. Its shallow coral gardens are well suited to snorkeling. Bring your passport: it is required at the park entrance. In the water, do not touch the coral or feed the fish: these are park rules.

If you are a certified diver, book a boat trip to Shark Reef and Yolanda Reef at the tip of Ras Mohammed National Park. In 1980, the Cypriot cargo ship Yolanda struck this reef while carrying a shipment of bathroom fixtures. A storm sent its hull sliding down to a depth of 160 m in 1987. The toilets, bathtubs, and sinks remained scattered across the sand, within divers’ reach. The current is often strong here: go with a dive center and a guide.

visits.text: It was at Qaitbay Fort in Rosetta, which the French called Fort Julien, that one of Bonaparte’s officers discovered the Rosetta Stone in July 1799. The stone bears the same decree from 196 BC inscribed three times: in hieroglyphs, Demotic (the everyday script used by Egyptians at the time), and Greek. Greek, which scholars could read, enabled Champollion to decipher the hieroglyphs in 1822. The original has been at the British Museum in London since 1802. Start the day at the fort, then head to the old town.

Facades of red, black, and white brick line the narrow streets of Rosetta’s old town, known as Rashid in Arabic. This decorative use of colored brick is almost unique in Egypt. Of the 38 houses listed as historic monuments in the early 20th century, 22 have survived and been restored. Two or three stories tall, they feature mashrabiyas, the ornate wooden screens that protect the windows. Look for Amasyali House, built in 1808, then Zaghloul Mosque, the oldest and largest in the city.

In Rosetta, look for Arab Killi House and view it from outside. The residence of an 18th-century Ottoman governor, it houses the Rashid National Museum. The ground floor contains a cistern and a sabil, a public fountain where passersby came to drink. The men’s floor opens onto a courtyard, while the women’s floor retains a cabinet inlaid with mother-of-pearl. In 2005, the British Museum gave Egypt a full-size replica of the Rosetta Stone, initially displayed in this museum. The museum is closed for restoration, so you can only view the house from outside.

If the light is fading, follow the Nile to Abu Mandour Mosque, built in 1897 on the riverbank. Rosetta lies near the mouth of one of the Nile’s two branches, where the river meets the Mediterranean. Enjoy the riverbanks before taking the road back to Alexandria, 65 km to the west.

visits.text: Domes, minarets, and facades with alternating bands of colored stone line al-Muizz Street, which stretches for about 1 km. Stop at the Sultan Qalawun complex, built in 1284 and 1285: it combined a madrasa, a mausoleum, and a hospital. The hospital treated patients for more than 500 years before being demolished in 1910. A combined ticket grants access to several monuments along the street, starting with Qalawun’s complex.

activities.text: If you can, walk along al-Muizz Street in the late afternoon, then again after dark, when modern lighting highlights the restored facades. Named after the Fatimid caliph al-Mu’izz li-Din Allah, it connects the gates of Bab al-Futuh and Bab Zuweila. Renovated beginning in 1997, it feels like an open-air museum as you walk through it. It is also known as Coppersmiths’ Street: hookahs and copperware are sold here.

places.name: Saint Catherine

visits.text: According to local history, the Jebeliya, Saint Catherine’s Bedouin tribe, descend from Roman soldiers who settled here in the 6th century. That was the century when Emperor Justinian had the nearby monastery built. Their village of El Milga is the starting point for hikes and the place to find guides. Use the evening to arrange your Mount Sinai ascent with them: departure time, headlamp, and warm clothing.

According to UNESCO, Saint Catherine, at the foot of Mount Sinai, is home to the oldest Christian monastery still serving its original purpose. Byzantine Emperor Justinian had it built between 548 and 565. Visits follow a fixed route: the Well of Moses, the main church, then the Burning Bush. Tradition holds that this bramble is the bush from which God spoke to Moses. The monastery is open from 9 a.m. to 11:30 a.m., except on Fridays, Sundays, and major Orthodox holidays. Guided tours are prohibited inside.

A mosque has stood within the grounds of Saint Catherine’s Monastery since 1106. It was created inside a chapel under the Fatimid dynasty, which ruled Egypt at the time. The monastery also holds the world’s second-largest collection of ancient manuscripts, after the Vatican’s. The Codex Sinaiticus, a handwritten Bible from the 4th century, was kept here for many years; it is now at the British Library in London. Only the church and its immediate surroundings are open to the public: stay on the designated route.

activities.text: Twelve fissures mark the Rock of Moses, halfway along Wadi el-Arbain, a dry valley that climbs from the village of Saint Catherine. Tradition identifies them as the twelve springs that burst forth when Moses struck the rock, an episode mentioned in the Quran. At the end of the valley, the Monastery of the Forty Martyrs, founded in the 6th century, is surrounded by olive trees, cypresses, and a large garden. Book your Bedouin guide in advance and set out in midafternoon to return before nightfall.

visits.text: Less famous than Giza, Saqqara still deserves a morning: this is where the history of the pyramids begins. The Step Pyramid of Djoser, built in the 27th century BC by the architect Imhotep, is described by UNESCO as the first pyramid ever built. Its six tiers rise to 62.5 m. It reopened in March 2020 after 14 years of restoration. No public transportation serves the site: arrive by taxi or rideshare when it opens at 8 AM.

Limestone columns arranged in pairs greet visitors at the entrance to Djoser’s funerary complex in Saqqara. This colonnade has 40 columns nearly 6 m tall. Around it, an enclosure wall 10.5 m high extends for more than 1.6 km. Farther on, the Heb-Sed court, lined with chapels, was intended for a royal ritual that Djoser was to perform in the afterlife. Allow 30 minutes for the Imhotep Museum at the site entrance.

places.name: Sharm El Sheikh

visits.text: Lively until late and set on a natural bay, Naama Bay is the tourist heart of Sharm el-Sheikh. The city remained under Israeli control from 1967 to 1982 before being returned to Egypt. Today, Naama Bay’s waterfront promenade is lined with cafés, restaurants, and bazaars. Come in the early evening, when the atmosphere is family-friendly. Bars and music take over later at night.

A white lighthouse, an offshore breeze, and a sea that shifts between shades of blue at the foot of the cliff: this is Ras Um Sid, a headland in Sharm el-Sheikh south of Naama Bay. Look for fossil imprints in the rock, traces of ancient marine organisms preserved in stone. Just below, a protected reef begins very close to shore: the corals are just a few swimming strokes from the beach. The lighthouse is generally closed to visitors. Save this headland for sunset, when the view stretches toward the Strait of Tiran.

Sharm el-Sheikh’s Old Market has more character than the streets of the beach resorts. Its stalls sell spices, fabrics, and handmade goods a few streets from Sharm El Maya harbor. Above the market rise the minarets of Al Sahaba Mosque, inaugurated in 2017. Its architect blended Ottoman, Fatimid, and Mamluk styles, representing three periods in the history of Muslim Egypt. Come at sunset, when the waterfront comes alive, and negotiate prices before buying.

activities.text: You will land at Sharm el-Sheikh International Airport, about 12 km from Naama Bay. Two visas are available at the counter. The free “Sinai Only” visa, valid for 15 days, does not allow you to leave South Sinai. According to several travel guides, it also does not cover access to Ras Mohammed by road. For this itinerary, get the Egypt visa, which costs 30 dollars in cash according to the French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs. Book your transfers with a driver as well: the same source advises against long journeys without someone who knows the route and speaks Arabic.

Set out early for the Strait of Tiran: boats leave Sharm el-Sheikh between 8 a.m. and 9 a.m. and reach the reefs in 60 to 90 minutes. Depending on the wind, the crew chooses one or more of the four reefs: Jackson, Woodhouse, Thomas, or Gordon. You may encounter turtles and sometimes dolphins. Tiran Island, visible from the boat, is uninhabited. It has belonged to Saudi Arabia since 2017. Make the most of the calmer morning: in the afternoon, the north wind creates small waves and strengthens the current.

Head to Sharm el-Sheikh International Airport, about 27 km from the Nabq reserve via the track and then the road. If you rented a car, return it at the airport counter. Otherwise, your driver will drop you off in front of the terminal. Keep your passport handy: you will be asked to show it at checkpoints along the road.

visits.text: The Great Sphinx of Giza was not built: it was carved directly into the plateau’s limestone. This lion with a human head measures 73 m long and 20 m high. Its nose is missing, and contrary to a persistent legend, Napoleon’s soldiers had nothing to do with it: the damage was already recorded in the 10th century. Tool marks suggest that it was deliberately removed. Egyptians call it Abu al-Hol, often translated as “the father of terror.” Keep your site ticket: it is checked at the entrance to the enclosure.

visits.text: According to local tradition, the Ben Ezra Synagogue stands on the spot where the baby Moses is said to have been found. The current building dates from the 1890s, but the synagogue is much older. Its geniza, a storeroom where the community accumulated old writings, contained around 400,000 documents that came to scholars’ attention in the late 19th century. Most are now held at Cambridge University Library. There are no longer any worshippers: the site can be visited as a small museum in 20 minutes.

places.name: Wadi El Natrun

visits.text: Start at the Monastery of Saint Bishoy (Deir Anba Bishoy), one of the four Coptic monasteries in Wadi El Natrun that are still inhabited. Copts are the Christians of Egypt. Saint Bishoy, a disciple of Saint Macarius, the valley’s first hermit, founded a community here in the late 4th century. In one corner of the enclosure stands the keep, a refuge tower rebuilt after a raid in 1096. The monks entered it by a drawbridge, which they raised during attacks. Admission is free; ask a monk to guide you and leave a donation.

The monks at the Monastery of the Syrians (Deir al-Suryan) are happy to show visitors a tamarind tree: according to legend, it grew from the staff that Saint Ephrem the Syrian had leaned against a door. The monastery owes its name to Syrian merchants who bought it in the early 8th century. In its Church of the Virgin, restorers uncovered several overlapping layers of murals in the 1990s. The oldest date back to the 7th century. It is just 500 m northwest of the Monastery of Saint Bishoy: walk there.
